extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalism scholars, and African newsroom practitioners/editors
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the news values, selection pressures, and production constraints shaping story selection and presentation in Ghanaian, Nigerian, and pan‑African newsrooms. Useful for researchers, editors, and practitioners diagnosing newsroom practices and recommending reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and crisis emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: War, crime, killings, crises, terrorism dominate coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage is skewed toward violent/conflictual events; stories that fit these frames are more likely to be selected than routine or positive developments. This pattern explains why audiences see Africa as crisis-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underrepresentation of development/progress stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of progress / development stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about development and positive local progress are regularly underweighted or omitted, leading to a skewed impression of national/regional realities; editors and reporters may deprioritize these given perceived audience interest or resource constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on international wire services
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy reliance on Western news agencies (BBC, Reuters, AP, AFP) for content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International wires supply a large share of copy; BBC World Service is universally consulted. This shapes framing and reduces indigenous sourcing and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited cross‑African correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited cross‑African correspondence and indigenous foreign reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few bureaus or local correspondents reporting across African countries mean pan‑African events are often covered only through external wires or not at all, reducing intra‑continental visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction of Western framing
rubrics_metrics.description: News coverage often reproduces Western frames rather than indigenous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on international sources and frames leads to stories framed through Western templates, which may omit local/development/anti‑colonial angles scholars argue should be foregrounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical constraints affecting reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Congested networks, slow internet, malfunctioning computers, lack of multimedia workstations limit reporting capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infrastructure problems constrain what can be produced (e.g., fewer multimedia or timely pieces), affecting story selection toward items that can be managed with limited tech resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner political and business interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners' political/business interests shape editorial choices and what gets published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners may block or steer coverage to protect investments or political ties; this pressure can result in systematic biases in story selection and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story killing and editorial restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Killed" stories and explicit restrictions on criticizing owner‑aligned figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain topics are suppressed internally; journalists learn which beats/topics are off-limits, shaping routine newsroom selection and self-censorship practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government pressure and self‑censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Political pressures from government create self‑censorship among journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear of reprisal or regulatory action leads reporters and editors to avoid sensitive topics or to temper criticism, reducing investigative and adversarial reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tribal / ethnic identity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Tribal and ethnic identity considerations influence story selection and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and reporters take ethnic affiliations into account to avoid inflaming tensions or to appeal to particular audience segments; balancing or favoring ethnic perspectives is a routine news value in many outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious significance (Christianity, Islam) is weighed in news decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories involving religious actors or themes are prioritized or framed differently; religious leader pronouncements are routinely newsworthy and can shape editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pan‑African solidarity vs. nation‑specific orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of pan‑African solidarity versus nation‑specific angles in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsrooms may choose frames emphasizing continental solidarity or national interests depending on audience, owner stance, and political context; this tension influences which regional stories receive prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diaspora connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Diaspora links (news relevant to citizens abroad or involving diaspora actors) are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that connect to migrant communities or diaspora networks get attention because of audience ties, remittance politics, and transnational influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development progress (sometimes underweighted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development progress is a recognized value but is often underweighted in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While development reporting is conceptually important, resource and framing pressures often mean progress stories are sidelined; some scholars argue for boosting development‑oriented coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti‑colonial framing opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are evaluated for their potential to advance anti‑colonial critiques or perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage that challenges neocolonial narratives or highlights indigenous agency can be favored as part of an explicitly post‑colonial editorial stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence of major political figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Major political figures are often overweighted in news selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personality‑centered reporting—elevating statements and actions of prominent politicians—drives coverage priorities, sometimes at the expense of policy or structural analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donor and international agency relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Donor / international agency news (NGOs, UN) is a routine news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage often privileges stories connected to donors or international agencies, reflecting funding flows, access, and newsroom source dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports importance (football central)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports—especially football—are centrally important in news selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High audience interest in football drives allocation of resources and story prominence, making sports a stable news value across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious leader pronouncements as news
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouncements by religious leaders are treated as inherently newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements from clerical authorities receive coverage because of their social influence; such items can take precedence over other civic or policy topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI and automation adoption in newsroom workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of AI (copy‑editing, ad targeting) is an emerging innovation shaping news production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption affects speed, content personalization, and editorial workflows; it may influence what is practical to produce and how stories are distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobile‑first distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Mobile‑first news strategies reflect that most readers access content via phones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Story formats, lengths, multimedia choices, and timing are adapted to mobile audiences; mobile constraints favor short, immediately engaging items and influence selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of messaging platforms (WhatsApp/SMS) for alerts
rubrics_metrics.description: WhatsApp and SMS alerts are used as primary distribution channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct messaging shapes editorial packaging (bite‑sized updates) and can drive story prioritization for rapid, shareable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local language broadcasting
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasting in local languages is an innovation and a routine editorial consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using indigenous languages expands reach and shapes story selection toward locally salient issues, requiring different sourcing and framing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen journalism integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen journalism (e.g., Sahara Reporters model) is a source and production model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User‑generated content and activist outlets supplement limited correspondent networks, affecting verification practices and the kinds of stories that surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owner safety (what won't get killed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions are influenced by concerns about owner safety and what content might be suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists anticipate which topics will be 'killed' to avoid jeopardizing owners' interests; this implicit criterion constrains investigative and critical reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for government pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Story selection is conditioned by how much government pressure a newsroom can tolerate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets factor in expected regulatory or political backlash when deciding whether to pursue sensitive stories, often choosing lower‑risk angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donor relevance as a newsworthiness filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance to donors or international agencies increases a story's chances of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because donors shape funding and visibility, stories that align with donor agendas or programs receive attention and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnic and religious balance requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms aim to maintain ethnic and religious balance in coverage to manage social tensions and audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors actively balance voices and beats to avoid alienating constituencies; this balancing act shapes beat assignment and story prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of wire content as a practical selector
rubrics_metrics.description: Available wire content determines what can be published, given resource constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When local reporting capacity is low, editors rely on readily-available wire copy—shaping both topics and framing around what is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local correspondent reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The geographic and institutional reach of local correspondents conditions which stories are feasible to cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outlets with limited correspondent networks will underreport areas/events outside their reach; correspondent presence drives beat salience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for indigenous, development‑ and peace‑oriented frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly critique: Western news values are inadequate; there is a need for development‑oriented, peace‑oriented, indigenous frameworks to better capture African newsroom realities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for reframing news values imply evaluation criteria should include contributions to development, peacebuilding, and local epistemologies rather than only Western norms.
